analysis.one_liner: Raises income tax rates on incomes above $1 million, up to 49% on the very largest.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised tax rates on households with taxable income above $1 million, never received a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created new, higher tax brackets for very high incomes: 45% on the portion of income between $1 million and $10 million, rising in steps to 49% on income over $1 billion. It would also have taken away the special low tax rate on capital gains for taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket, so their investment profits would be taxed like other income. The bill received no action after being referred to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who does not have taxable income over $1 million would pay nothing more under the bill, and a more progressive tax code would shift more of the federal tax burden onto the wealthiest households. The bill does not direct the additional revenue to any specific program, so its benefit to ordinary households runs through the general federal budget.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates new brackets beginning at $1 million of taxable income, at 45%, rising to 46%, 47%, and 48% at higher thresholds, and 49% on income over $1 billion.
Taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket would lose the lower capital gains tax rate, so their net capital gains would be taxed at ordinary income rates.

The top pre-existing bracket (incomes above roughly $379,150) returns to the 39.6% rate that applied before the 2001 tax cuts, so the bill also affects incomes between about $379,000 and $1 million, not only millionaires.
The bill was introduced with no Republicans; all 22 cosponsors were Democrats, so its chances in a House controlled by the other party were low from the start.

analysis.who_pays: Households with taxable income above roughly $379,000, and above all those above $1 million, would pay higher taxes. Investors, including fund managers and large shareholders, whose gains fall in the 45% bracket would pay ordinary income rates on those gains instead of the lower capital gains rate.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the top rate to 39.6% for all taxable income above roughly $379,150, so it reaches high-earning but sub-millionaire households, not just the very wealthy.

By removing the capital gains preference for taxpayers in the 45% bracket, the bill would tax large investment gains at rates as high as 49%, which supporters of lower capital gains rates argue discourages the realization of investment gains and the capital that funds businesses. That trade-off is inherent to the bill's design; the bill text itself provides the rate recapture.
The bill raises revenue without earmarking it for any specific purpose, so taxpayers could not see what, if anything, they got in return.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's costs fall entirely on households with taxable income above roughly $379,000, with the steepest new rates on income above $1 million. For the roughly 99% of households below those thresholds, it would impose no new tax. The main honest trade-off is the loss of the capital gains preference at the very top, which critics say could dampen investment activity; the counterargument is that those gains would simply be taxed as ordinary income, as wages already are.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky and nine other House Democrats introduced the Fairness in Taxation Act of 2011 on March 16, 2011.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 112th Congress.
The bill drew 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of them were enough to move it out of committee; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with taxable income above $1 million, whose income would have been taxed at rates up to 49%, are better off because the bill never advanced. Investors relying on the lower capital gains rate also keep that preference.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup during the two-year Congress

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controlled the House and its committee agenda in the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill or any version of it to the floor at any point

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 22 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill, so the fight followed party lines from introduction to death.

industries.note: The bill would impose rates of 45% to 49% on income above $1 million and eliminate the capital gains preference at that level. Its defeat leaves current lower rates in place for this group.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: These investors earn much of their income as capital gains, which the bill would tax at ordinary rates up to 49% for those in the top new brackets. They keep the lower capital gains rate because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: High-income professionals and business owners ($379,000-$1 million)
industries.note: Even below $1 million, this group's top rate would have returned to 39.6% under the bill's rate table. For most of them the change is modest relative to the changes at higher incomes.
